children.text: A wildlife sanctuary on an island north of Busuanga, where giraffes and zebras brought over from Kenya in
still roam freely today. You can even get up close to the endangered Calamian deer, making it a great change of pace for a day trip during a Coron holiday.

Calauit Safari Park (formally the Calauit Game Preserve and Wildlife Sanctuary) is a roughly 3,700-hectare wildlife reserve covering all of Calauit Island, just across a narrow strait from the northwestern tip of Busuanga Island in the Calamian Islands of northern Palawan. It was established by presidential decree under the Marcos government in

. The park began when eight species of African animals — giraffes, zebras, elands, impalas, waterbucks, gazelles, topis, and bushbucks, 104 animals in all — were shipped in by boat from Kenya and released here in

At the time, Kenya was struggling to protect its wildlife amid drought and poaching, and the Philippines presented this as an international conservation project. Over the decades, many species failed to adapt to the climate and environment and died out, but giraffes and zebras have bred across several generations and still roam the island's grasslands today. As of around
, the park is home to about 20 giraffes and around 30 zebras.

The park also plays an important role in conserving species native to the Philippines. The Calamian deer, found only in the Calamian Islands, has grown from around 25 animals at the start of the conservation project to more than 1,000, and the park also protects the Philippine crocodile, Palawan bearded pig, binturong (bearcat), and Philippine mouse-deer. It has been managed by the Palawan provincial government since

If a Coron trip is usually built around lakes, limestone islands, and wreck diving, Calauit offers a completely different experience. Getting close enough to feed a giraffe from your hand in the early morning is a moment that stays with adults and children alike. It's a great choice for family travellers, animal lovers, or anyone who wants a day of rest between sea-based itineraries.

The park's history has a darker side too. The island was originally home to about 250 households, including indigenous Tagbanua people, who were relocated to other islands when the park was created. After the change of government in
, the budget was cut sharply and staff numbers fell from around 300 at one point to about 30, and the waterbuck, eland, impala, topi, bushbuck, and gazelle had all disappeared by around
. In
, the government handed the Tagbanua community the title deeds to Calauit Island and the surrounding waters. According to Philippine Information Agency (PIA) reports in early

, the only African animals remaining are 18 reticulated giraffes and 27 Grevy's zebras, all of them born on the island. There is no dedicated veterinarian and inbreeding is a problem, so bringing in new animals is a long-term challenge, but that same year the giraffe feeding area was renovated with a new steel gazebo, and renovation of the mini zoo also began.

If you time your visit for the morning feeding, a keeper will hand you a bundle of leaves so you can feed the giraffes yourself. You'll get to watch, right up close, as a giraffe curls its long tongue around the leaves to pull them in.
Ride an open-top truck or jeepney across the grasslands in search of herds of zebra and deer. This usually comes with an extra fee (around
This small, shy native deer gathers in herds along the edge of the grassland and the forest line. Approach quietly and you can spot dozens at once.
Visit the enclosures for native species — the Philippine crocodile, binturong, porcupine, Palawan bearded pig — with a guide's commentary.
The trip begins with a short bangka crossing of about
5–10 minutes
from Makalachao Pier at the northwestern tip of the main island of Busuanga to Calauit Island. On clear days the water is an emerald green.
Many Calauit tours are packaged together with Black Island (Malajon), just off the coast of Busuanga. After lunch, a boat ride of about
30 minutes
takes you to a white-sand beach beneath black limestone cliffs, where you can swim, snorkel, and explore caves; on the way back, it's common to stop at Malbato Church and Busuanga town.

You can see native animals such as the Philippine crocodile, Philippine porcupine, Palawan bearded pig, binturong, turtles, and birds of prey up close in their enclosures. The park also takes in and cares for wildlife from the Calamian Islands that has been turned over to the Palawan Council for Sustainable Development (PCSD), and renovation of the mini zoo began in

When you enter, you receive a numbered ticket, and when your turn comes you step inside the enclosure and give the giraffes the leaves a keeper hands you. Because the people are inside the pen and the giraffes are outside, it's safe, and each session takes about
10 minutes
. Hold a generous handful of leaves up high, and the giraffe will lower its head toward you.
Pickup from your hotel in Coron town (this varies by tour operator). Board the van and head northwest across Busuanga Island.

by van, you reach Makalachao Pier in the village of Salvacion and cross to Calauit Island by bangka (

Tour the grasslands by safari truck, looking for zebras and Calamian deer, then visit the mini zoo.
Return to the mainland for lunch. Many tours stop at the Buluang Fish Farm restaurant.
Take a boat to Black Island for swimming, snorkeling, and a look at the caves.

to the pier, and because the road is winding and bumpy, motorbikes are recommended only for experienced riders.

Leave the park and eat near the pier, then decide on your afternoon plans. Allowing time to get back to Coron before dark, set out no later than
Staying at a beach resort in northern Busuanga instead of Coron town cuts travel time to around
1 hour
, letting you enter the park during the quietest early-morning hours.
It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Clark to Busuanga Airport (USU, Coron), with several flights a day by Philippine Airlines, Cebgo (a Cebu Pacific affiliate), and Sunlight Air. There are also direct flights from Cebu.

The 2GO large ferry from Manila to Coron (about
13–18 hours
) sails about twice a week, with fares of about
in Super Value class. Cancellations and delays due to weather are frequent, so if your schedule is tight, flying is the realistic option.
From El Nido to Coron by fast craft takes about
4 hours
and costs about
per person; departures are usually around 12:00 PM.
From Coron town, most travelers take a travel agency's joiner tour (van, boat, entrance fee, and lunch included). It costs about
per person.
If you go independently, you have to charter a van (about
per vehicle) and hire a boat separately at Makalachao Pier, so unless you are a group of four or more, a joiner tour is more economical.
Within Coron town, a single tricycle ride costs about
. Inside the park, the only way to get around is by safari truck.
Makalachao Pier (Salvacion, Busuanga), across from Calauit Island, is about
2 hours
by road from Coron town and about
1 hour 30 minutes
from Busuanga Airport.
From the pier to Calauit Island it's
5–10 minutes
by boat, and the boat fare and entrance fee are paid separately. Part of the road is unpaved, so it takes longer when it rains.
The dry season, from
November
to
May
, is the best time to visit. During this period, the roads in northern Busuanga are in good condition and the sea is calm, making the pier crossing easy.
December–February
is especially cool, making even a midday safari bearable.
March–May
is hot and the grasslands turn a dry gold, making the landscape look even more like an African savanna.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon brings frequent rain, and unpaved sections can turn muddy, lengthening travel times. The Calamian Islands can fall within typhoon paths some years, so it's essential to check the forecast between
July–November
. Regardless of season, the animals are most active during the morning feeding and just after sunrise, so an early visit is best.
Temperatures in northern Busuanga range from
throughout the year, and annual rainfall is about 2,800 mm. The rainy season brings frequent rain, and in
July–August
strong winds persist and boats stop running on some days. Joiner tour seats fill up quickly in the high season, so it's safest to book as soon as you arrive in Coron.

Most travellers stay in Coron town and visit Calauit as a day trip. Coron town has everything from guesthouses at around
a night to mid-range hotels in the

range, and it's also convenient for reaching Maquinit Hot Spring or the Mount Tapyas viewpoint. If you'd prefer somewhere quieter, you can also spend a night or two in northern Busuanga or at an island resort, in which case meals are usually taken care of at the resort.

There are no proper restaurants inside the park, so check whether lunch is included in your tour, or, if travelling independently, bring a packed lunch and water from Coron town. In Coron town, you can enjoy cashews (a Palawan specialty), coconut crab (a protected species best avoided), fresh grilled fish and kinilaw, and mango shakes made with Busuanga mangoes. Seafood restaurants near the market let you pick items by weight and have them cooked to order.

Joiner tour lunches are often at the Buluang Fish Farm restaurant in Busuanga town. If your tour doesn't include lunch, or you're visiting independently, bring a packed lunch and water from near the market in Coron town. There is almost no accommodation near Calauit, so the usual approach is to make it a day trip and return to Coron or Busuanga town.
Giraffe feeding usually happens in the morning, so choose as early a tour as possible.
Most of the trip is spent in a vehicle, so motion sickness medication and a neck pillow help. Some stretches of road are still bumpy and winding.
There's no shade on top of a safari truck, so a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen are essential.
A giraffe's long tongue may touch your hand when you feed it, so bring wet wipes, and a wide-angle lens works better than a telephoto for close-up giraffe photos.
Coron town has ATMs, but there are none in northern Busuanga or inside the park, so bring cash for the entrance fee and tips.
When booking a joiner tour, check carefully whether the entrance fee, truck fee, lunch, and Ditaytayan Island entrance fee are included, to avoid extra costs on the day.
If travelling with children, pack plenty of snacks and water given the long drive.

Rather than scheduling Calauit right after arriving in Coron, it works well as a rest-day activity between lake and lagoon hopping tours. Since Calauit involves little time on the water, it's also easier on companions prone to seasickness.
Deer and zebras are sensitive to noise. When you get off the truck to observe them, avoid loud noises and move slowly to get a longer, closer look.
Giraffe feeding turns go in order of entry, so tours that arrive early in the morning have shorter waits. Check your turn number before boarding the safari truck.
Zebras are not for feeding, and they can bite or kick. Do not touch or chase any animal, and follow the keepers' instructions.
Giraffes and zebras are close to their wild state. Don't approach or stand behind them in places the keepers haven't permitted — zebras in particular can deliver a dangerous kick.
Feeding the animals snacks or human food other than what the keepers provide is prohibited.
The park's entrance fee and operating hours (generally
8 AM–5 PM
) can change under provincial government policy, so check the latest notice.
During the rainy season, flooded roads and suspended boat service can lead to tour cancellations. Build a spare day into your Coron itinerary.
Mosquitoes can be plentiful, so bring insect repellent and long sleeves.
Commercial filming, drones, and camping inside the park require separate permission and fees. Check with the park office beforehand.
